chapters.title: Chapter 2: Building Blocks: Randomness, Volatility, and Brownian Motion

lessons.title: Volatility: Historical vs Implied, and Why It Drives Option Prices

children.text: The One Input Nobody Can Observe Directly

Of the six inputs from Chapter 1's pricing table, spot price is on your screen, strike and time to expiry are written into the contract, and the risk-free rate is published by the RBI and money markets every day. Volatility, σ, is different. Nobody quotes it anywhere. You have to estimate it, and there are exactly two honest ways to do that: look backward at how much the stock has actually moved, or look at what the options market is already paying to insure against future moves.

Historical volatility takes a series of past daily returns, computes their standard deviation, and scales that daily figure up to an annual one. Here is a tiny, illustrative five-day series to see the mechanics; a real calculation would use at least 20 to 252 trading days.

These five returns average to exactly 0%, which keeps the arithmetic clean: each return's deviation from the mean is just the return itself. Squaring them gives 4, 1, 1, 4, and 0, summing to 10. Dividing by 4 (one less than the number of observations, the standard convention for a sample) gives a variance of 2.5, so the daily standard deviation is the square root of 2.5, about 1.58%.

body.caption: 252 is the standard count of Indian trading days in a year (NSE and BSE combined calendar). Volatility scales with the square root of time, not time itself, a direct consequence of the σ√T term in the lognormal formula from the last lesson.

body.label: Illustrative 5-day historical volatility, annualized
body.context: 1.58% × √252 ≈ 1.58% × 15.87 ≈ 25.1%. This five-day sample is only for showing the mechanics; five data points are far too few to trust in practice.

body.title: Annualize it yourself
body.prompt: A stock's daily historical volatility, computed from its returns, is 1.2%. Using √252 ≈ 15.87, what is its annualized volatility, in percent?

children.text: Implied Volatility: Reading the Market's Own Estimate

Implied volatility runs the whole process backward. Instead of computing σ from past returns and feeding it into a pricing formula, take the option's live, quoted market premium, and ask: what value of σ would the Black-Scholes formula need to reproduce this exact price? There is no clean algebraic way to isolate σ from the formula, so this is solved numerically, trying values of σ until the formula's output matches the market price closely enough. The result is not a measurement of the past. It is the market's collective, real-money estimate of how volatile the underlying will be between now and expiry.

body.label: India VIX
body.context: Computed from the live order book of Nifty index options, India VIX represents the market's expectation of Nifty's annualized volatility over the next 30 calendar days. It moves every second the market is open and is the closest thing India has to a single headline number for "how nervous are options traders right now."

children.text: Backward-Looking vs Forward-Looking, in One Chart
The two measures often disagree, and the gap is most visible around a known event, such as the Union Budget or an RBI policy decision.

body.title: Illustrative pattern around a Budget day (not actual historical data)

body.text: Implied volatility climbs before the event because the market is pricing in the uncertainty of what is about to happen. Historical volatility barely moves in advance, because nothing volatile has actually happened yet. Right after the event, implied volatility often collapses fast, an effect traders call an IV crush, even while historical volatility only starts rising a week later, once that one big day is inside its trailing lookback window. The two measures are answering different questions: one about the future, one about the past.

body.title: Buying options ahead of the Budget
body.scenario: Ananya sees India VIX has jumped from 15 to 24 in the week before the Union Budget. She reasons: "Volatility is clearly elevated, so a big Nifty move is coming. I'll buy a straddle now and profit from the swing." She buys the day before the Budget, and Nifty does move meaningfully on Budget day, in line with what she expected.
body.prompt: Even though Ananya was right that Nifty would make a meaningful move, explain why she could still lose money on this trade.
body.modelAnswer: Ananya bought when India VIX, the implied volatility, was already at 24, meaning the market had already priced in a large move. Her straddle's premium was inflated by that anticipation. For the trade to profit, Nifty's actual move needs to exceed what an implied volatility of 24 was already pricing in, not just be "meaningful" in an everyday sense. The day after the event, implied volatility typically crushes back down toward its pre-event level regardless of how large the move was, since the uncertainty is now resolved. If Nifty's actual move was sizeable but smaller than what a 24% implied volatility had priced in, both the IV crush and the ordinary passage of time (theta decay, covered in Chapter 4) can erase her position's value even though her market call was directionally and magnitude-wise reasonable. Buying volatility ahead of a well-flagged event means buying it at its most expensive.

body.title: Which measure is which
body.question: A trading desk says, "Our model shows the stock moved with 18% annualized volatility over the past month, but the option chain is pricing 26%." Which number is historical and which is implied?
options: Both numbers are historical, just calculated differently
Both numbers are implied, just from different option chains
body.explanation: "Moved with 18% volatility over the past month" is a backward-looking calculation from realized returns: historical volatility. "The option chain is pricing 26%" is volatility backed out of current option premiums: implied volatility. Here the market is pricing in more future uncertainty than the recent past has actually shown.

body.text: Historical volatility tells you how volatile the underlying has been. Implied volatility tells you how volatile the market currently expects it to be. Black-Scholes needs the second one, and the market's own option prices are the only place to find it.

points: Volatility is the only Black-Scholes input that isn't directly observable; it must be estimated, either from the past or from current option prices.
Historical volatility is the standard deviation of past returns, annualized by multiplying by √252 (a direct consequence of the σ√T scaling in geometric Brownian motion).
Implied volatility is solved backward: the σ that makes Black-Scholes reproduce the option's actual live market price, found numerically since the formula cannot be algebraically inverted for σ.
India VIX is NSE's headline implied volatility index, derived from the Nifty index options order book, representing expected annualized volatility over the next 30 days.

The two measures diverge most around known events: implied volatility rises in anticipation and often crushes afterward, while historical volatility only rises once the event's move enters its trailing lookback window.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The five-day return series, the annualized volatility figures, and the Budget-day chart are hypothetical illustrations of volatility mechanics, not live market data or a recommendation to trade around any specific event. Always check the live India VIX and option chain on NSE or your broker's terminal.
